specStatements.text: Charles Darwin, as a result of observations on a round the world expedition, backed by years of experimentation and discussion and linked to developing knowledge of geology and fossils, proposed the theory of evolution by natural selection. Individual organisms within a particular species show a wide range of variation for a characteristic.; Individuals with characteristics most suited to the environment are more likely to survive to breed successfully.; The characteristics that have enabled these individuals to survive are then passed on to the next generation.
Darwin published his ideas in On the Origin of Species (1859). There was much controversy surrounding these revolutionary new ideas.

The theory of evolution by natural selection was only gradually accepted because: the theory challenged the idea that God made all the animals and plants that live on Earth; there was insufficient evidence at the time the theory was published to convince many scientists; the mechanism of inheritance and variation was not known until 50 years after the theory was published.

Other theories, including that of Jean-Baptiste Lamarck, are based mainly on the idea that changes that occur in an organism during its lifetime can be inherited. We now know that in the vast majority of cases this type of inheritance cannot occur.
A study of creationism is not required.
Students should be able to: describe the work of Darwin and Wallace in the development of the theory of evolution by natural selection; explain the impact of these ideas on biology.

Alfred Russel Wallace independently proposed the theory of evolution by natural selection. He published joint writings with Darwin in 1858 which prompted Darwin to publish On the Origin of Species (1859) the following year.
Wallace worked worldwide gathering evidence for evolutionary theory. He is best known for his work on warning colouration in animals and his theory of speciation.
Alfred Wallace did much pioneering work on speciation but more evidence over time has led to our current understanding of the theory of speciation.
Students should be able to describe the steps which give rise to new species.

Students should be able to: describe the development of our understanding of genetics including the work of Mendel; understand why the importance of Mendel's discovery was not recognised until after his death.

In the mid-19th Century Gregor Mendel carried out breeding experiments on plants. One of his observations was that the inheritance of each characteristic is determined by 'units' that are passed on to descendants unchanged.
In the late 19th Century behaviour of chromosomes during cell division was observed.
In the early 20th Century it was observed that chromosomes and Mendel's 'units' behaved in similar ways. This led to the idea that the 'units', now called genes, were located on chromosomes.
In the mid-20th Century the structure of DNA was determined and the mechanism of gene function worked out.
This scientific work by many scientists led to the gene theory being developed.
Students should be able to describe the evidence for evolution including fossils and antibiotic resistance in bacteria.
The theory of evolution by natural selection is now widely accepted.

Evidence for Darwin's theory is now available as it has been shown that characteristics are passed on to offspring in genes. There is further evidence in the fossil record and the knowledge of how resistance to antibiotics evolves in bacteria.
Fossils are the 'remains' of organisms from millions of years ago, which are found in rocks.

Fossils may be formed: from parts of organisms that have not decayed because one or more of the conditions needed for decay are absent; when parts of the organism are replaced by minerals as they decay; as preserved traces of organisms, such as footprints, burrows and rootlet traces.

Many early forms of life were soft-bodied, which means that they have left few traces behind. What traces there were have been mainly destroyed by geological activity. This is why scientists cannot be certain about how life began on Earth.
We can learn from fossils how much or how little different organisms have changed as life developed on Earth.
Students should be able to extract and interpret information from charts, graphs and tables such as evolutionary trees.
Extinctions occur when there are no remaining individuals of a species still alive.
Students should be able to describe factors which may contribute to the extinction of a species.
Bacteria can evolve rapidly because they reproduce at a fast rate.

Mutations of bacterial pathogens produce new strains. Some strains might be resistant to antibiotics, and so are not killed. They survive and reproduce, so the population of the resistant strain rises. The resistant strain will then spread because people are not immune to it and there is no effective treatment.
MRSA is resistant to antibiotics.

To reduce the rate of development of antibiotic resistant strains: doctors should not prescribe antibiotics inappropriately, such as treating non-serious or viral infections; patients should complete their course of antibiotics so all bacteria are killed and none survive to mutate and form resistant strains; the agricultural use of antibiotics should be restricted.
The development of new antibiotics is costly and slow. It is unlikely to keep up with the emergence of new resistant strains.

scopeNotes.statement: A study of creationism is not required.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: No concept, misconception or question in this set teaches, assesses or evaluates creationism. Where the specification requires the reasons why the theory of evolution by natural selection was only gradually accepted, this set uses AQA's own wording only - that the theory challenged the idea that God made all the animals and plants that live on Earth - and goes no further into religious belief.

concepts.definition: The process by which individuals with characteristics most suited to the environment are more likely to survive to breed successfully, so that the characteristics which have enabled these individuals to survive are then passed on to the next generation. Charles Darwin proposed the theory of evolution by natural selection as a result of observations on a round the world expedition, backed by years of experimentation and discussion and linked to developing knowledge of geology and fossils.

The differences between individuals of the same species. Individual organisms within a particular species show a wide range of variation for a characteristic, and this variation is already present in the population before natural selection acts on it.
The book in which Darwin published his ideas about evolution by natural selection in 1859. There was much controversy surrounding these revolutionary new ideas.

The theory of evolution by natural selection was only gradually accepted because the theory challenged the idea that God made all the animals and plants that live on Earth, because there was insufficient evidence at the time the theory was published to convince many scientists, and because the mechanism of inheritance and variation was not known until 50 years after the theory was published.

Another theory of how species change, proposed by Jean-Baptiste Lamarck, based mainly on the idea that changes that occur in an organism during its lifetime can be inherited. We now know that in the vast majority of cases this type of inheritance cannot occur.

The scientist who independently proposed the theory of evolution by natural selection. He published joint writings with Darwin in 1858 which prompted Darwin to publish On the Origin of Species (1859) the following year. Wallace worked worldwide gathering evidence for evolutionary theory and is best known for his work on warning colouration in animals and his theory of speciation.
The formation of new species. Alfred Wallace did much pioneering work on speciation, but more evidence over time has led to our current understanding of the theory of speciation.

concepts.term: Steps that give rise to a new species
concepts.definition: Populations of a species become isolated from one another and experience different conditions. There is variation within each population, and natural selection means that individuals with the characteristics most suited to their own environment are more likely to survive to breed successfully and pass those characteristics on. Over many generations the two populations become so different that they can no longer interbreed to produce fertile offspring, so they are two species.

In the mid-19th Century Gregor Mendel carried out breeding experiments on plants. One of his observations was that the inheritance of each characteristic is determined by 'units' that are passed on to descendants unchanged.

concepts.term: Why Mendel's discovery was not recognised in his lifetime
concepts.definition: Mendel worked in the mid-19th Century, before the behaviour of chromosomes during cell division had been observed, so there was no known structure that could carry his 'units'. The significance of his discovery was therefore not appreciated by scientists at the time and was only recognised after his death.

In the late 19th Century the behaviour of chromosomes during cell division was observed. In the early 20th Century it was observed that chromosomes and Mendel's 'units' behaved in similar ways, and this led to the idea that the 'units', now called genes, were located on chromosomes.

concepts.term: Structure of DNA and gene theory
concepts.definition: In the mid-20th Century the structure of DNA was determined and the mechanism of gene function was worked out. This scientific work by many scientists led to the gene theory being developed.

Evidence for Darwin's theory is now available as it has been shown that characteristics are passed on to offspring in genes. There is further evidence in the fossil record and in the knowledge of how resistance to antibiotics evolves in bacteria. Because of this evidence the theory of evolution by natural selection is now widely accepted, which is the impact these ideas have had on biology.
The 'remains' of organisms from millions of years ago, which are found in rocks.

Fossils may be formed from parts of organisms that have not decayed because one or more of the conditions needed for decay are absent, when parts of the organism are replaced by minerals as they decay, or as preserved traces of organisms, such as footprints, burrows and rootlet traces.

concepts.term: Gaps in the early fossil record
concepts.definition: Many early forms of life were soft-bodied, which means that they have left few traces behind. What traces there were have been mainly destroyed by geological activity. This is why scientists cannot be certain about how life began on Earth.

A diagram, built from evidence such as the fossil record, in which a branch point shows a common ancestor shared by the organisms on the branches above it. Evolutionary trees and other charts, graphs and tables let us learn from fossils how much or how little different organisms have changed as life developed on Earth.
Extinctions occur when there are no remaining individuals of a species still alive.

A species may become extinct because of changes to the environment over geological time, new predators, new diseases, new more successful competitors, or a single catastrophic event such as a massive volcanic eruption or a collision with an asteroid.
Bacteria can evolve rapidly because they reproduce at a fast rate.

Mutations of bacterial pathogens produce new strains. Some strains might be resistant to antibiotics, and so are not killed. They survive and reproduce, so the population of the resistant strain rises. The resistant strain will then spread because people are not immune to it and there is no effective treatment.
A strain of bacteria which is resistant to antibiotics.

concepts.term: Reducing the development of resistant strains
concepts.definition: To reduce the rate of development of antibiotic resistant strains, doctors should not prescribe antibiotics inappropriately, such as treating non-serious or viral infections; patients should complete their course of antibiotics so all bacteria are killed and none survive to mutate and form resistant strains; and the agricultural use of antibiotics should be restricted.
The development of new antibiotics is costly and slow. It is unlikely to keep up with the emergence of new resistant strains.

misconceptions.question: A population of mice lives in a cold place. Over many generations the mice come to have thicker fur. How does this happen?
misconceptions.correct: Mice that already had thicker fur were more likely to survive to breed successfully, so the characteristic was passed on to the next generation.
misconceptions.misconception: Each mouse grows thicker fur during its own lifetime because of the cold, and then passes that thicker fur on to its offspring.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Lamarck's idea matches everyday experience of bodies responding to their surroundings, such as muscles growing with use, and it feels more purposeful and tidier than selection acting on variation that is already there.
misconceptions.correction: Other theories, including that of Jean-Baptiste Lamarck, are based mainly on the idea that changes that occur in an organism during its lifetime can be inherited. We now know that in the vast majority of cases this type of inheritance cannot occur. Individuals with characteristics most suited to the environment are more likely to survive to breed successfully, and it is those characteristics that are then passed on to the next generation.

misconceptions.question: Why do plants growing in a dry habitat have deeper roots than related plants in a wet habitat?
misconceptions.correct: Individuals with deeper roots were more likely to survive to breed successfully, so this characteristic was passed on to the next generation.
misconceptions.misconception: The plants needed more water, so they made themselves grow deeper roots; evolution gives organisms the characteristics they need.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Everyday language such as 'the plant adapted to reach water' suggests organisms change on purpose, so students give the process an aim that it does not have.
misconceptions.correction: Evolution by natural selection has no aim. Individual organisms within a particular species show a wide range of variation for a characteristic, and individuals with characteristics most suited to the environment are more likely to survive to breed successfully.

misconceptions.question: Where does the variation come from that natural selection acts on?
misconceptions.correct: It is already there: individual organisms within a particular species show a wide range of variation for a characteristic.
misconceptions.misconception: A change in the environment creates the new characteristic, which the organisms then use to survive.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Selection is only noticed once the environment changes, so students treat the environmental change as the maker of the characteristic rather than as the filter acting on characteristics that already exist.
misconceptions.correction: Individual organisms within a particular species show a wide range of variation for a characteristic. The environment does not create the characteristic; individuals with characteristics most suited to the environment are more likely to survive to breed successfully.

misconceptions.question: How quickly was the theory of evolution by natural selection accepted?
misconceptions.correct: Only gradually - there was much controversy surrounding these revolutionary new ideas when Darwin published On the Origin of Species in 1859.
misconceptions.misconception: The evidence in Darwin's book was so strong that scientists accepted the theory as soon as it was published in 1859.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Timelines present 1859 as the moment evolution became established science, which hides the decades of argument and the missing evidence that followed publication.
misconceptions.correction: There was much controversy surrounding these revolutionary new ideas. The theory was only gradually accepted because it challenged the idea that God made all the animals and plants that live on Earth, because there was insufficient evidence at the time the theory was published to convince many scientists, and because the mechanism of inheritance and variation was not known until 50 years after the theory was published.

misconceptions.question: Did Darwin know how characteristics are passed on when he published his theory?
misconceptions.correct: No. The mechanism of inheritance and variation was not known until 50 years after the theory was published.
misconceptions.misconception: Darwin explained natural selection using genes and DNA, so he already knew how characteristics are inherited.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Natural selection and genetics are taught in the same topic, so students assume both sets of ideas were available to scientists at the same time.
misconceptions.correction: The mechanism of inheritance and variation was not known until 50 years after the theory was published. Mendel's 'units' were only called genes and located on chromosomes in the early 20th Century, and the structure of DNA was determined in the mid-20th Century. Evidence for Darwin's theory is now available as it has been shown that characteristics are passed on to offspring in genes.

misconceptions.question: What was Alfred Russel Wallace's role in the theory of evolution by natural selection?
misconceptions.correct: He independently proposed the theory of evolution by natural selection and published joint writings with Darwin in 1858.
misconceptions.misconception: Wallace worked for Darwin, collecting specimens abroad so that Darwin could write his own theory.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Darwin's name dominates every account of evolution, so a second name in the same story is read as a helper rather than as an independent scientist reaching the same theory.
misconceptions.correction: Alfred Russel Wallace independently proposed the theory of evolution by natural selection. He published joint writings with Darwin in 1858 which prompted Darwin to publish On the Origin of Species (1859) the following year, and he worked worldwide gathering evidence for evolutionary theory.

misconceptions.question: Two isolated populations of one species now look noticeably different. Are they two species?
misconceptions.correct: Not necessarily. They are two species only once they can no longer interbreed to produce fertile offspring.
misconceptions.misconception: As soon as two groups of organisms look clearly different from each other they are two separate species.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Species are usually introduced to students through pictures and appearance, so looking different is taken as the test for being a different species.
misconceptions.correction: Populations become isolated and experience different conditions, and natural selection selects different characteristics in each population. Over many generations the two populations become so different that they can no longer interbreed to produce fertile offspring. Alfred Wallace did much pioneering work on speciation but more evidence over time has led to our current understanding of the theory of speciation.

misconceptions.question: What did Mendel discover in his breeding experiments on plants?
misconceptions.correct: That the inheritance of each characteristic is determined by 'units' that are passed on to descendants unchanged.
misconceptions.misconception: Mendel discovered genes and DNA, and showed that genes are carried on chromosomes.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Mendel's work is usually retold using the modern words gene and DNA, so students credit him with concepts that were only developed much later.
misconceptions.correction: One of Mendel's observations was that the inheritance of each characteristic is determined by 'units' that are passed on to descendants unchanged. Only in the early 20th Century was it observed that chromosomes and Mendel's 'units' behaved in similar ways, leading to the idea that the 'units', now called genes, were located on chromosomes; the structure of DNA was determined in the mid-20th Century.

misconceptions.question: Why was the importance of Mendel's discovery not recognised until after his death?
misconceptions.correct: Because the behaviour of chromosomes during cell division had not yet been observed, so there was no known structure that could carry his 'units'.
misconceptions.misconception: Mendel's results were shown to be wrong at the time, or he never published them, so nobody took any notice.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students look for a fault in the work itself to explain why it was overlooked, rather than for a missing piece of supporting science elsewhere.
misconceptions.correction: In the mid-19th Century Mendel carried out breeding experiments on plants. In the late 19th Century behaviour of chromosomes during cell division was observed, and in the early 20th Century it was observed that chromosomes and Mendel's 'units' behaved in similar ways. Without that later work the significance of his discovery could not be appreciated in his lifetime.

misconceptions.question: What happens to most organisms after they die?
misconceptions.correct: They decay, so they do not form fossils; fossils form only when the usual conditions for decay are disturbed.
misconceptions.misconception: Any organism that dies and is buried will eventually turn into a fossil in the rock.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Museums and textbooks show large numbers of fossils, so fossilisation looks like the normal fate of a dead organism rather than a rare event.
misconceptions.correction: Fossils are the 'remains' of organisms from millions of years ago, which are found in rocks. Fossils may be formed from parts of organisms that have not decayed because one or more of the conditions needed for decay are absent, when parts of the organism are replaced by minerals as they decay, or as preserved traces of organisms.

misconceptions.question: Is a preserved dinosaur footprint a fossil?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. Fossils may be formed as preserved traces of organisms, such as footprints, burrows and rootlet traces.
misconceptions.misconception: Fossils have to be part of the organism's body, such as bones, teeth or shells, so a footprint does not count.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word 'remains' is read as body parts, and the fossils on display in museums are usually skeletons, so traces are not recognised as fossils.
misconceptions.correction: Fossils may be formed as preserved traces of organisms, such as footprints, burrows and rootlet traces, as well as from parts that have not decayed and from parts replaced by minerals as they decay.

misconceptions.question: Why can scientists not be certain about how life began on Earth?
misconceptions.correct: Because many early forms of life were soft-bodied and left few traces, and those traces have been mainly destroyed by geological activity.
misconceptions.misconception: The fossil record holds a fossil of every organism that has lived, so the origin of life is already fully known.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Evolutionary trees are drawn as complete, unbroken branching diagrams, which gives the impression that the fossil record has no gaps in it.
misconceptions.correction: Many early forms of life were soft-bodied, which means that they have left few traces behind. What traces there were have been mainly destroyed by geological activity. This is why scientists cannot be certain about how life began on Earth.

misconceptions.question: An evolutionary tree shows two species alive today meeting at a branch point. What does the branch point mean?
misconceptions.correct: It represents a common ancestor from which both of the present-day species descended.
misconceptions.misconception: One of the two species alive today is the ancestor, and the other one evolved from it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Trees are read like a family tree of parents and children, so a species drawn next to or below another is taken to be its ancestor.
misconceptions.correction: An evolutionary tree lets us learn how much or how little different organisms have changed as life developed on Earth. A branch point represents an ancestor shared by the organisms on the branches above it, not one present-day species descending from another.

misconceptions.question: What does it mean to say that a species is extinct?
misconceptions.correct: There are no remaining individuals of that species still alive.
misconceptions.misconception: A species is extinct when its numbers have fallen very low and only a few individuals are left.
misconceptions.whyItArises: News reports use 'extinct' and 'endangered' loosely and often interchangeably, so the two words become blurred.
misconceptions.correction: Extinctions occur when there are no remaining individuals of a species still alive.

misconceptions.question: Which factors may contribute to the extinction of a species?
misconceptions.correct: Changes to the environment over geological time, new predators, new diseases, new more successful competitors, or a single catastrophic event.
misconceptions.misconception: Species only become extinct because of human activity such as hunting or clearing habitats.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Almost every extinction reported in the media today is caused by people, so other causes acting over geological time are overlooked.
misconceptions.correction: Factors which may contribute to the extinction of a species include changes to the environment over geological time, new predators, new diseases, new more successful competitors, and a single catastrophic event such as a massive volcanic eruption or a collision with an asteroid.

misconceptions.question: How does a population of antibiotic resistant bacteria arise?
misconceptions.correct: Mutations of bacterial pathogens produce new strains; resistant strains are not killed, so they survive and reproduce and the population rises.
misconceptions.misconception: The antibiotic changes the bacteria so that they become resistant to it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Resistance is noticed after antibiotics have been used, so the antibiotic is taken to be the cause of the change rather than the thing selecting between strains that already differ.
misconceptions.correction: Mutations of bacterial pathogens produce new strains. Some strains might be resistant to antibiotics, and so are not killed. They survive and reproduce, so the population of the resistant strain rises. Bacteria can evolve rapidly because they reproduce at a fast rate.

misconceptions.question: Should a doctor prescribe antibiotics for a patient with a viral infection?
misconceptions.correct: No. Doctors should not prescribe antibiotics inappropriately, such as treating non-serious or viral infections.
misconceptions.misconception: Antibiotics will help with any infection, including viral illnesses such as colds and flu.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Antibiotics are the most familiar prescribed medicine for feeling ill, and patients often expect them whatever the cause of the illness.
misconceptions.correction: To reduce the rate of development of antibiotic resistant strains, doctors should not prescribe antibiotics inappropriately, such as treating non-serious or viral infections.

misconceptions.question: Why should a patient complete a course of antibiotics?
misconceptions.correct: So that all bacteria are killed and none survive to mutate and form resistant strains.
misconceptions.misconception: Once the symptoms have gone the infection is over, so the rest of the tablets are not needed.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Feeling better is taken as proof that every bacterium has already been killed, so the remaining doses seem pointless.
misconceptions.correction: Patients should complete their course of antibiotics so all bacteria are killed and none survive to mutate and form resistant strains.

misconceptions.question: Can developing new antibiotics solve the problem of resistance on its own?
misconceptions.correct: No. The development of new antibiotics is costly and slow and is unlikely to keep up with the emergence of new resistant strains.
misconceptions.misconception: Scientists can simply develop a new antibiotic whenever a resistant strain appears.
misconceptions.whyItArises: New medicines are reported as sudden breakthroughs, which hides the cost and the many years of development behind them.
misconceptions.correction: The development of new antibiotics is costly and slow. It is unlikely to keep up with the emergence of new resistant strains, so the use of antibiotics must also be controlled.

mcqs.stem: In a beetle population, shell thickness varies. Predators cannot eat the thickest-shelled beetles. After many generations most beetles have thick shells. Why?

options.text: Beetles grew thicker shells in life and passed them on.
options.rationale: A student who believes changes made during an organism's lifetime can be inherited picks this. We now know that in the vast majority of cases this type of inheritance cannot occur.

options.text: Thick-shelled beetles survived to breed and passed this on.
options.rationale: Individuals with characteristics most suited to the environment are more likely to survive to breed successfully, and the characteristics that have enabled these individuals to survive are then passed on to the next generation.

options.text: Beetles needed thicker shells, so they grew them to survive.
options.rationale: A student who believes organisms change on purpose picks this. Evolution by natural selection has no aim; it acts on variation that is already present in the population.

options.text: Predators made thick shells appear in the beetle population.
options.rationale: A student who believes the environment creates characteristics picks this. Individual organisms within a particular species already show a wide range of variation for a characteristic; the predators only decide which variants survive to breed.

mcqs.stem: Which of these is a reason why the theory of evolution by natural selection was only gradually accepted?

options.text: Scientists in 1859 were at once convinced by the evidence.
options.rationale: A student who believes the theory was accepted at once picks this. There was much controversy surrounding these revolutionary new ideas, and there was insufficient evidence at the time the theory was published to convince many scientists.

options.text: The mechanism of inheritance was not known for 50 more years.
options.rationale: The mechanism of inheritance and variation was not known until 50 years after the theory was published, which is one of the reasons given for the theory being only gradually accepted.

options.text: Lamarck had shown that changes made in life are inherited.
options.rationale: A student who accepts Lamarck's idea picks this. Lamarck's idea was never shown to be correct; we now know that in the vast majority of cases this type of inheritance cannot occur.

options.text: Darwin had already explained inheritance in terms of genes.
options.rationale: A student who believes Darwin knew about genes picks this. Mendel's 'units' were only called genes and located on chromosomes in the early 20th Century, long after On the Origin of Species was published in 1859.

mcqs.stem: Giraffes with longer necks can reach more leaves. How would a biologist today explain why giraffes now have long necks?

options.text: Reaching high leaves created the long neck characteristic.
options.rationale: A student who believes the environment creates characteristics picks this. Variation in neck length was already present in the population; feeding conditions only decide which giraffes survive to breed.

options.text: Necks stretched during life were passed to the offspring.
options.rationale: This is Lamarck's idea, based mainly on the idea that changes that occur in an organism during its lifetime can be inherited. We now know that in the vast majority of cases this type of inheritance cannot occur.

options.text: Giraffes needed longer necks, so their necks became longer.
options.rationale: A student who believes organisms change because they need to picks this. Evolution by natural selection has no aim and organisms cannot choose their characteristics.

options.text: Giraffes with longer necks survived and bred more often.
options.rationale: Individuals with characteristics most suited to the environment are more likely to survive to breed successfully, and those characteristics are then passed on to the next generation.

mcqs.stem: What was Alfred Russel Wallace's contribution to the theory of evolution by natural selection?

options.text: He collected specimens overseas for Darwin's new book.
options.rationale: A student who thinks Wallace worked for Darwin picks this. Wallace did work worldwide gathering evidence, but he did so for his own work and independently proposed the theory himself.

options.text: He explained natural selection using genes and DNA.
options.rationale: A student who believes the mechanism of inheritance was known at the time picks this. The mechanism of inheritance and variation was not known until 50 years after the theory was published.

options.text: He proposed the same theory independently of Darwin.
options.rationale: Alfred Russel Wallace independently proposed the theory of evolution by natural selection and published joint writings with Darwin in 1858, which prompted Darwin to publish On the Origin of Species the following year.

options.text: He convinced other scientists to accept the theory.
options.rationale: A student who believes the theory was accepted at once picks this. There was much controversy surrounding these revolutionary new ideas and the theory was only gradually accepted.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about the theory of speciation is correct?

options.text: More evidence has changed our understanding over time.
options.rationale: Alfred Wallace did much pioneering work on speciation but more evidence over time has led to our current understanding of the theory of speciation.

options.text: Wallace gathered the evidence for Darwin's own ideas.
options.rationale: A student who thinks Wallace assisted Darwin picks this. Wallace worked worldwide gathering evidence for evolutionary theory and is best known for his own work on warning colouration and his theory of speciation.

options.text: Two groups are new species once they look different.
options.rationale: A student who judges species by appearance picks this. Two populations are separate species only once they can no longer interbreed to produce fertile offspring.

options.text: Wallace's ideas on speciation were accepted at once.
options.rationale: A student who believes new theories are accepted immediately picks this. More evidence over time has led to our current understanding of the theory of speciation.

mcqs.stem: Two populations of one snail species are separated by a new river. What must finally happen for them to become two different species?

options.text: They must look different enough to be told apart by eye.
options.rationale: A student who judges species by appearance picks this. Populations of one species can look very different and still interbreed to produce fertile offspring.

options.text: They must change during life and pass these changes on.
options.rationale: A student holding Lamarck's idea picks this. We now know that in the vast majority of cases this type of inheritance cannot occur; natural selection passes on inherited characteristics.

options.text: They must not be able to breed to give fertile young.
options.rationale: The isolated populations experience different conditions, so natural selection selects different characteristics in each. Over many generations they become so different that they can no longer interbreed to produce fertile offspring, and they are then two species.

options.text: The river must create new characteristics in each group.
options.rationale: A student who believes the environment creates characteristics picks this. Variation is already present in each population and the different conditions only select between the variants that are there.

mcqs.stem: What did Mendel conclude from his breeding experiments on plants?

options.text: That genes made of DNA are carried on the chromosomes.
options.rationale: A student who credits Mendel with modern genetics picks this. The 'units' were only called genes and located on chromosomes in the early 20th Century, and the structure of DNA was determined in the mid-20th Century.

options.text: That the environment creates a plant's characteristics.
options.rationale: A student who believes the environment creates characteristics picks this. Mendel's breeding experiments showed that each characteristic is determined by 'units' passed on to descendants.

options.text: That plant breeding could not explain inheritance.
options.rationale: A student who assumes Mendel's work failed picks this. His breeding experiments did explain inheritance, but their importance was not recognised until after his death.

options.text: That 'units' pass on each characteristic unchanged.
options.rationale: One of Mendel's observations was that the inheritance of each characteristic is determined by 'units' that are passed on to descendants unchanged.

mcqs.stem: Why was the importance of Mendel's discovery not recognised until after his death?

options.text: His breeding results were later shown to be incorrect.
options.rationale: A student who assumes the work was faulty picks this. Mendel's observations were correct; what was missing was the later scientific work that could explain them.

options.text: He had described genes before DNA had been discovered.
options.rationale: A student who credits Mendel with genes picks this. Mendel described 'units', and only in the early 20th Century were these called genes and located on chromosomes.

options.text: His work was accepted by other scientists straight away.
options.rationale: A student who believes new ideas are accepted immediately picks this. The importance of Mendel's discovery was not recognised until after his death.

options.text: The behaviour of chromosomes had not yet been seen.
options.rationale: Mendel worked in the mid-19th Century. Behaviour of chromosomes during cell division was only observed in the late 19th Century, and only in the early 20th Century was it observed that chromosomes and Mendel's 'units' behaved in similar ways.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about the development of our understanding of genetics is correct?

options.text: Darwin used genes to explain variation when he published.
options.rationale: A student who believes Darwin knew the mechanism of inheritance picks this. That mechanism was not known until 50 years after the theory was published.

options.text: Chromosome behaviour was observed after Mendel's work.
options.rationale: Mendel carried out his breeding experiments in the mid-19th Century; in the late 19th Century behaviour of chromosomes during cell division was observed, and in the early 20th Century it was observed that chromosomes and Mendel's 'units' behaved in similar ways, leading to the idea that the 'units', now called genes, were located on chromosomes.

options.text: Mendel discovered DNA during his experiments on plants.
options.rationale: A student who credits Mendel with modern genetics picks this. The structure of DNA was determined in the mid-20th Century, about a century after Mendel's experiments.

options.text: Mendel's 'units' were rejected once chromosomes were seen.
options.rationale: A student who assumes Mendel's work was discarded picks this. Observing that chromosomes and Mendel's 'units' behaved in similar ways supported his work and led to the idea that the 'units' were located on chromosomes.

mcqs.stem: What happened in the mid-20th Century in the development of gene theory?

options.text: Mendel described the first genes made of DNA in plants.
options.rationale: A student who credits Mendel with genes and DNA picks this. Mendel worked in the mid-19th Century and described 'units', not genes made of DNA.

options.text: Darwin's theory explained inheritance by using genes.
options.rationale: A student who believes Darwin knew about genes picks this. The mechanism of inheritance and variation was not known until 50 years after his theory was published.

options.text: Mendel's 'units' were proved wrong by chromosome work.
options.rationale: A student who assumes Mendel's work was overturned picks this. Work on chromosomes supported the 'units' and led to them being called genes and located on chromosomes.

options.text: The structure of DNA and gene function were worked out.
options.rationale: In the mid-20th Century the structure of DNA was determined and the mechanism of gene function worked out. This scientific work by many scientists led to the gene theory being developed.

mcqs.stem: Which observation is evidence that supports the theory of evolution by natural selection?

options.text: Antibiotic resistance evolves in bacterial populations.
options.rationale: Evidence for Darwin's theory is now available in the fossil record and in the knowledge of how resistance to antibiotics evolves in bacteria, and it has been shown that characteristics are passed on to offspring in genes. The theory is now widely accepted.

options.text: Dead organisms are turned into fossils in the rocks.
options.rationale: A student who thinks fossilisation is the usual fate of a dead organism picks this. Most organisms decay; fossils form only when one or more of the conditions needed for decay are absent, when parts are replaced by minerals, or as preserved traces.

options.text: Animals that exercise pass strength to their young.
options.rationale: A student holding Lamarck's idea picks this. We now know that in the vast majority of cases this type of inheritance cannot occur, so it is not evidence for natural selection.

options.text: The fossil record gives us a complete history of life.
options.rationale: A student who thinks the fossil record has no gaps picks this. Many early forms of life were soft-bodied and left few traces, and those traces have been mainly destroyed by geological activity.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about how fossils are formed is correct?

options.text: Bones and shells are kept, but footprints are not.
options.rationale: A student who thinks a fossil must be a body part picks this. Fossils may also be formed as preserved traces of organisms, such as footprints, burrows and rootlet traces.

options.text: A dead organism will turn into a fossil in the rock.
options.rationale: A student who thinks fossilisation is the normal fate of a dead organism picks this. Fossils form only in particular conditions, for example when one or more of the conditions needed for decay are absent.

options.text: Traces such as footprints and burrows are preserved.
options.rationale: Fossils may be formed as preserved traces of organisms, such as footprints, burrows and rootlet traces, as well as from undecayed parts and from parts replaced by minerals as they decay.

options.text: The fossil record includes each species from the past.
options.rationale: A student who thinks the fossil record has no gaps picks this. Many early forms of life were soft-bodied, so they have left few traces behind.

mcqs.stem: Why can scientists not be certain about how life began on Earth?

options.text: Scientists have now collected the earliest fossils.
options.rationale: A student who thinks the fossil record is complete picks this. Traces of early life have been mainly destroyed by geological activity, so the record of the earliest organisms is very incomplete.

options.text: Early organisms had bones which dissolved in rocks.
options.rationale: A student who thinks fossils must be hard body parts picks this. Many early forms of life were soft-bodied, so they had no bones to preserve in the first place.

options.text: Early life was soft-bodied and left few traces behind.
options.rationale: Many early forms of life were soft-bodied, which means that they have left few traces behind, and what traces there were have been mainly destroyed by geological activity.

options.text: Early organisms became fossils that we can study.
options.rationale: A student who thinks every dead organism fossilises picks this. Soft-bodied early organisms left few traces, and most of those have been destroyed by geological activity.

mcqs.stem: An evolutionary tree shows species P and Q meeting at a branch point, with species R branching off much earlier. What does the tree show?

options.text: P and Q share a more recent common ancestor than R.
options.rationale: A branch point on an evolutionary tree represents an ancestor shared by the organisms above it, so the later the branch point, the more recently the organisms shared an ancestor and the less they have changed from each other.

options.text: Species Q evolved directly from species P over time.
options.rationale: A student who reads the tree like a family tree of parents and children picks this. P and Q are both present-day species; the branch point is the ancestor they share, not one of them.

options.text: P and Q are separate species as they look different.
options.rationale: A student who judges species by appearance picks this. Species are separate once they can no longer interbreed to produce fertile offspring, which the tree does not show directly.

options.text: The tree shows each of the species that has lived.
options.rationale: A student who thinks the fossil record is complete picks this. Many early forms of life were soft-bodied and left few traces, so trees are built from an incomplete record.

mcqs.stem: A species of bird disappears from Earth after a volcanic eruption destroys its habitat. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The species is extinct once its numbers fall very low.
options.rationale: A student who confuses extinct with endangered picks this. Extinctions occur when there are no remaining individuals of a species still alive.

options.text: Human hunting is what makes a species become extinct.
options.rationale: A student who thinks people are the sole cause of extinction picks this. Extinction may also follow environmental change, new predators, new diseases, new competitors or a catastrophic event.

options.text: Fossils show the exact date each species died out.
options.rationale: A student who thinks the fossil record is complete picks this. Few early organisms left traces and many traces have been destroyed by geological activity.

options.text: A catastrophic event can cause a species to die out.
options.rationale: Extinctions occur when there are no remaining individuals of a species still alive, and a single catastrophic event such as a massive volcanic eruption is one of the factors which may contribute to extinction.

mcqs.stem: A patient's MRSA infection is not killed by an antibiotic. Why has the population of the resistant strain risen?

options.text: Resistant bacteria survived and reproduced rapidly.
options.rationale: Some strains produced by mutation might be resistant to antibiotics, and so are not killed. They survive and reproduce, so the population of the resistant strain rises, and bacteria can evolve rapidly because they reproduce at a fast rate.

options.text: The antibiotic changed the bacteria so they resist it.
options.rationale: A student who thinks the antibiotic causes resistance picks this. Mutations of bacterial pathogens produce new strains; the antibiotic only kills the strains that are not resistant.

options.text: The bacteria needed to resist, so they became resistant.
options.rationale: A student who believes organisms change because they need to picks this. Resistance arises by mutation, and evolution by natural selection has no aim.

options.text: Each bacterium became resistant and passed this on.
options.rationale: A student holding Lamarck's idea picks this. The bacteria do not change themselves during their lives; resistant strains are produced by mutation and are then selected.

mcqs.stem: Which action would reduce the rate of development of antibiotic resistant strains?

options.text: Prescribing antibiotics to treat viral infections.
options.rationale: A student who thinks antibiotics work on any infection picks this. Doctors should not prescribe antibiotics inappropriately, such as treating non-serious or viral infections.

options.text: Restricting the use of antibiotics in agriculture.
options.rationale: The agricultural use of antibiotics should be restricted, which is one of the measures given for reducing the rate of development of antibiotic resistant strains.

options.text: Stopping a course of antibiotics when symptoms go.
options.rationale: A student who thinks the course can end with the symptoms picks this. Patients should complete their course of antibiotics so all bacteria are killed and none survive to mutate and form resistant strains.

options.text: Relying on new antibiotics being developed quickly.
options.rationale: A student who expects new medicines to arrive on demand picks this. The development of new antibiotics is costly and slow and is unlikely to keep up with the emergence of new resistant strains.
